ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Source text (鎮州臨濟慧照禪師語錄), file T/T47/T47n1985.xml; exact actor: Linji Yixuan. The full-case proof distinguishes this actor from nearby respondents, questioners, and section subjects.

Senses.Explanation: The isolated four graphs say, 'stop (歇)—that is (即) awakening (菩提),' but the corpus's recurring full quotation supplies the omitted subject: 'the crazed mind does not stop; when it stops, that is awakening' (狂心不歇，歇即菩提). A historical compendium follows the phrase with its own explicit explanation, beginning 'as for “when it stops, that is awakening”' and describing what it calls awakening. Chan masters repeatedly take up the quoted line in hall discourse. One says that when dust-labor suddenly stops, 'when it stops, that is awakening,' then immediately asks the assembly, 'from where is it obtained?' Another says people run north, south, east, and west for years without a place to stop and asks, 'can you people stop?' The Zen deviation is the quotation's deployment as a public teaching-seat proposition and direct question. Restoring its attested subject avoids turning every kind of ceasing into the roadmap's broad 'ceasing itself is enlightenment.'
